items.title: Covert Assistance: Helpful LLM Agents Evade Oversight in Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: As multi-agent systems enter high-stakes domains, the possibility that agents may circumvent safety boundaries is a growing concern. Prior work has examined this risk primarily in adversarial settings, where agents are instructed or rewarded to communicate covertly and evade oversight. We show that benign agents can cross the same boundaries without adversarial incentives. We emulate a software-engineering workflow in which a planner represents a company hiring an external developer. The planner writes requirements and holds a company credential it is instructed not to disclose to the developer; a monitor screens their exchanges. Seven of nine tested frontier models disguise the credential in their requirements to help the developer recover it while evading the monitor, even after completing their assigned objective. For example, across 6,000 episodes with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, the planner attempts concealment in 16.9%; in 0.9%, the credential evades the monitor and is recovered and used by the developer. Despite the low per-episode rate, the risk compounds across repeated exchanges: at 0.9%, 105 independent episodes carry a 61.3% chance of at least one breach. Our analysis suggests that the planner misinterprets disguised disclosure as helping the developer and reads the nondisclosure rule as banning plaintext, not character codes or riddles. We call this behavior covert assistance. Monitoring favors concealment, while concealment gives way to direct disclosure when the recipient is presented as a human rather than an AI agent, so leakage persists. Giving the monitor the credential improves detection but requires trusting it with the secret. These risks, in models already used for software engineering, challenge oversight to distinguish authorized cooperation from task-advancing assistance that crosses safety boundaries.

items.title: CRAFT: Exploring Wearable Creative AI on Smart Glasses for Fiction Writing in Real-World Contexts
items.abstract: Creative writing increasingly integrates AI assistance, yet current tools miss in-situ moments when writers draw inspiration from real-world experiences. We envision Context-aware Reality-Fiction Transformation ( CRAFT ), an approach for AI glasses that translates daily experiences into fiction narratives. We explored its desirability, feasibility, and potential viability through three studies. Interviews with nine writers yielded desires and three design goals: 1) augmenting in-situ perception to bridge reality-fiction gaps, 2) promoting authenticity grounded in real-world experiences while maintaining fictionalization, and 3) preserving creative agency, enjoyment, and life-art boundaries. Co-design workshops with 16 writers and researchers operationalized these goals into concrete interaction mechanisms using a technology probe. We then conducted supported field trials with eight writers across 24 sessions using a refined probe, revealing writer-perceived benefits (e.g., enriched fictional ideas from serendipitous encounters), emergent practices (e.g., micro-creation), and design considerations for future sustained use. We contribute design explorations for the CRAFT approach, offering design implications and empirical insights on ubiquitous human-AI creative collaboration in everyday life.

items.title: DAIMON: Designing AI-Augmented Research Dashboards to Enable Novel Human-AI Collaborative Workflows in Longitudinal Sensing Studies
items.abstract: Researchers conduct longitudinal passive sensing studies in in-the-wild settings, often spanning months or years, to uncover naturalistic behavioral patterns. These studies are not “set-and-forget” deployments; they require continuous monitoring as technical failures and declining participant compliance can lead to substantial missing data, undermining study validity and downstream models. Thus, conducting these studies involves multiple detail-oriented, cognitively demanding, and time-consuming tasks, making it a burdensome and stressful process. Existing research dashboards, the primary tools for data monitoring, offer limited support in easing this burden. Leveraging recent advances in AI for passive sensing data, we explore the design of human-AI collaborative workflows enabled through research dashboards to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of monitoring and associated tasks. We begin with a co-design study with 13 researchers involved in longitudinal sensing studies to identify desired AI capabilities and interactions through semi-structured interviews, brainstorming, and sketching activities. We operationalize novel human-AI workflows our participants envisioned by implementing an AI-augmented dashboard prototype DAIMON , and use it as a research probe in two studies: a task-based study and a deployment within an ongoing real-world sensing study. Our findings demonstrate the promise of AI-augmented dashboards in supporting researchers' day-to-day data monitoring and decision-making tasks. It also surfaces concerns around transparency and expectations with AI systems. Consolidating insights across all three studies, we present design guidelines for AI-augmented dashboards for longitudinal passive sensing research and discuss directions for future work.

items.title: Dampak Implementasi Rekam Medis Elektronik Terhadap Beban Kerja Dan Well-Being Tenaga Kesehatan: Suatu Tinjauan Sistematis
items.abstract: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) have become an essential component of healthcare digital transformation, but their implementation may also increase healthcare workers’ workload and affect their well-being. This review aimed to systematically analyze the impact of EHR implementation on healthcare workers’ workload and well-being based on recent scientific evidence. A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Literature searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library to identify studies published between 2020 and 2025 using the PECO framework. The selection process identified 20 studies that met the predefined inclusion criteria and were subsequently synthesized using a narrative approach. The review found that EHR implementation consistently increased documentation burden, prolonged digital working hours, and elevated cognitive workload due to system complexity. Poor EHR usability was also associated with higher levels of work-related stress, burnout, emotional exhaustion, reduced job satisfaction, and impaired work–life balance among healthcare workers. The magnitude of these effects varied according to professional role, healthcare setting, and individual characteristics, including gender. Overall, EHR implementation provides important benefits for improving healthcare quality; however, it may also increase workload and reduce healthcare workers’ well-being when system usability is inadequate and digital tasks extend beyond regular working hours. Therefore, optimizing EHR design, simplifying documentation workflows, and limiting after-hours digital work are essential to support the long-term well-being of the healthcare workforce.

items.title: Death of Human Style of Writing in the World of AI
items.abstract: Abstract: The Artificial Intelligence (AI) writing tools like ChatGPT and Claude have changed the world of official and unofficial communication in last two to three years. The human style of writing is diminishing and there is a rise of only one universal writing style created by the AI tools which lack human expressions and creativity. The AI tools are rampantly used by students, researchers, writers and people in general for any kind of serious as well as casual writing today. The excessive use of AI tools in writing is also responsible for reducing human ability of logical and critical thinking. Therefore, there is an urgency of using AI writing tools wisely so that the human writing skills get enhanced and the tools prove to be a boon. This research paper examines the challenges posed by AI writing tools and discusses how the AI can be used effectively and responsibly to enhance human writing skills.

items.title: Debias It Yourself: Teaching LLMs Cognitive Bias Mitigation Interventions
items.abstract: Bias has long been studied in social psychology and cognitive science, where decades of research have produced a body of validated interventions that reduce stereotypical thinking and prejudiced responses in humans. We propose Debias It Yourself (DIY), a cognitively grounded framework that translates five such interventions into debiasing procedures for large language models and delivers them through three established paradigms: Show (in-context examples), Train (instruction tuning), and Revise (guided self-revision). Across three models, five bias benchmarks, eleven debiasing baselines, and three reasoning benchmarks, Train+Revise and Revise alone attain the top two average ranks, lead the bias-reasoning tradeoff (mean bias as low as 2% at 90% reasoning accuracy), and reduce bias on unseen dimensions by up to 14.8%. Our code and data are publicly available.

items.title: Delegating Knowledge: Belief in AI Sufficiency and its Consequences for How People Process Information
items.abstract: Generative AI produces information on demand, raising the question of why one would ever learn something that a chatbot can always retrieve. In this paper, we introduce Belief in AI Sufficiency (BAS): the belief that acquiring and retaining knowledge is less valuable because AI can provide it when needed. BAS represents a qualitatively distinct conceptual domain from the Google effect, cognitive offloading, and the “News Finds Me” perception. Using four preregistered studies in the United States (development, N = 307; validation, N = 903; experiment, N = 767; test-retest, N = 298), we present evidence for a 12-item BAS measure with a strong general factor structure. In the validation survey, higher BAS was associated with greater reliance on heuristic and less systematic processing, and with reduced factual knowledge. In the experiment, BAS strongly predicted the likelihood to delegate a learning task to AI. The relationship between BAS and the gap between self-reported and measured knowledge was smaller, reflecting reduced accuracy rather than an illusion of knowledge. Finally, BAS scores were approximately equal in mean level and showed moderate rank-order stability across a 3-month period. BAS is one way to measure how far AI is becoming central to the study of how people learn.

items.title: Delovne obremenitve v dobi umetne inteligence: raziskovalni trendi
items.abstract: Research Question (RQ): How has research on AI and workload developed over time, and what themes, methods, and gaps shape current understanding of workload and well-being in AI-enabled work? Purpose: The purpose of this study is to map and describe the research landscape on AI and workload, identifying key topics, publication trends, and gaps relevant to work design, management, and well-being. Method: The study applies bibliometric analysis to peer-reviewed publications indexed in Scopus over the last five years. A transparent search strategy covers AI, workload, and related concepts. The analysis examines publication growth, citation patterns, source and author networks, and keyword co-occurrence, supported by science-mapping techniques. Interpretation is guided by work-design and job demands perspectives. Results: We found strong growth in publications across the AI and workload cross-section and high interdisciplinarity of the field. We reveal dominant research themes, the concentration of research across regions, and methodological patterns, as well as areas that remain understudied in relation to AI, workload, and well-being. Organization: By synthesizing a fragmented body of research, the study helps managers and HR professionals understand where evidence on the use of AI is well-developed and where caution or further evaluation is needed when implementing AI in work processes. Society: Clarifying how workload is addressed in AI-related research contributes to responsible AI use, worker health, and fair work practices in increasingly automated environments. Originality: The study offers a focused bibliometric overview of AI-related workload research, bringing together interdisciplinary perspectives on work design, stress, and well-being that are often studied separately. Limitations / further research: Bibliometric findings depend on coverage of a single database and on search choices and do not provide causal evidence. Future research should combine bibliometric mapping with empirical and intervention studies across sectors and regions.

items.abstract: This exploratory, design-oriented pilot case study examines Erwin, a student-centred AI scaffold designed to augment students’ thinking in an interdisciplinary design innovation module. Unlike answer-giving chatbots, Erwin adopts a supportive-critic stance: it provides stage-aware, dialogic scaffolding that widens idea spaces and supports criteria-based consolidation through nudges and commitments. The analysis drew on 1,999 student and Erwin turns organised into 171 sessions nested within 78 student logs, alongside post-module qualitative feedback. The study combined reflexive thematic analysis with a full-corpus, non-inferential descriptive analysis of selected interaction-process indicators, including initiative balance, futures probes, completed repair sequences, and system boundary or refusal episodes. A purposive sample of six final artefacts provided illustrative triangulation of interaction patterns and student project trajectories. The analysis identified four practices: disciplined divergence, in which Deliberate Cognitive Friction (DCF) prompts appeared alongside expanded frames without displacing agency; criteria-aware convergence, in which students translated broadened views into clearer problem statements, constraints, and next steps; cognitive resilience visible through repair and persistence sequences; and a supportive-critic experience shaped by answer resistance and meta-reflection. As this was a single-course pilot with no control condition, the descriptive indicators characterise observed interaction processes and contextualise the qualitative interpretation; they are not estimates of causal effects or direct measures of learning outcomes. Across cases, these practices appeared alongside traces of broadened ideation, criteria-guided consolidation, and futures-oriented reasoning in the illustrative artefact sample. The paper contributes situated empirical evidence for studying AI as human augmentation rather than substitution; a transferable design blueprint that operationalises DCF at the prompt policy layer through explainable prompts, resilience guardrails, and instrumentation for scaffolding-oriented LLM systems; and a process-oriented operationalisation of cognitive resilience for Human Computer Interaction in education, understood as interactional evidence of repair, persistence, and flexible reframing rather than as a demonstrated learning effect. The discussion offers implications for designing resilient, trust-preserving human-AI ecosystems that balance augmentation against risks of overreliance and cognitive offloading.

items.title: Determining key approaches to enhancing the survivability of armored vehicle crews, considering the use of situational awareness systems in modern warfare
items.abstract: The study aims to provide a theoretical rationale for key approaches to enhancing the survivability of armored vehicle crews–incorporating situational awareness systems–and to develop a novel method for assessing the extent to which these systems contribute to the crew's defensive response. The methodological framework combines systems, structural-functional, comparative, and criteria-based approaches, alongside a content analysis of scholarly works, the decomposition of the situational awareness cycle, and a custom point-based assessment method. Crew survivability is viewed as the outcome of the coordinated operation of systems for observation, threat detection, identification and prioritization, information exchange, decision support, protection, and the restoration of control following adverse impacts. It is established that situational awareness serves a preventive function within the survivability system of armored vehicles, as it shifts the initiation of the defensive response to a stage preceding the actual impact. A six-criterion assessment system is proposed, covering the continuity and completeness of observation, timeliness of detection, resilience of information support, quality of prioritization, integration of information exchange, and the capacity to sustain the crew's defensive response. A 0–4 point scale and an integral index are used to compare the conceptual approaches. The scientific novelty lies in interpreting situational awareness as a functional component of ensuring crew survival through preventive measures and in formulating the "perception–recognition–assessment–decision–protective reaction" sequence as an object of theoretical evaluation. The practical significance of the results stems from their potential application in substantiating modernization directions for armored weaponry and equipment, preliminarily comparing information support options, and establishing development priorities for situational awareness systems.

items.title: Developing an AI Governance Readiness Index (AIGRI) for Indian Higher Education Institutions
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education with intelligent learning systems, automated administration, research support, academic assessment, and institutional decision-making. As Indian Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) increasingly incorporate AI-enabled technologies, the lack of a standardized framework for evaluating institutional readiness for responsible AI governance has become a significant policy and administrative challenge. Current evaluation mechanisms primarily emphasize digital infrastructure and technology adoption, neglecting critical aspects such as ethical governance, institutional policy, regulatory compliance, data governance, academic integrity, human capacity development, and transparency, accountability, and risk management. In this paper, we propose developing an AI Governance Readiness Index (AIGRI) as a multidimensional framework to evaluate the preparedness of Indian Higher Education Institutions for the responsible and sustainable adoption of AI. The proposed index is structured around eight interconnected dimensions: Institutional Leadership and Governance, AI Policy and Regulatory Compliance, Digital Infrastructure, Data Governance and Cybersecurity, Human Capacity and AI Literacy, Ethical and Responsible AI Practices, Academic and Research Integrity, and Continuous Evaluation and Innovation. Each dimension is associated with measurable indicators that enable institutions to assess their current status, identify governance gaps, and formulate evidence-based strategies for improvement. The study employs a qualitative doctrinal and policy research approach, underpinned by an extensive review of national education policies, AI governance frameworks, international ethical AI guidelines, and literature on higher education quality assurance. The paper proposes a preliminary scoring model based on principles of responsible AI, good governance, and institutional accountability, which can then be validated through empirical research with universities across India. The proposed AIGRI is a practical governance tool for university administrators, policymakers, accreditation agencies, and regulatory bodies to assess AI readiness systematically. It also contributes to the emerging discourse of AI governance by shifting the focus from technology adoption to institutional preparedness, ethical implementation, and governance maturity. The framework could be a valuable addition to national quality assurance efforts, such as NAAC. It could be aligned with India’s vision of digitally empowered, globally competitive, and socially responsible higher education institutions. The study concludes that the development of a standardized AI Governance Readiness Index can guide policy decisions, enhance institutional resilience, encourage responsible AI adoption, and aid sustainable transformation of higher education in the era of intelligent technologies.

items.title: Development and Validation of the Occupational Safety Awareness Scale for Motorcycle Couriers
items.abstract: Motorcycle couriers in the platform-based gig economy are exposed to substantial occupational risks, yet no validated instrument exists to measure their occupational health and safety (OHS) awareness. This study develops and validates the Occupational Safety Awareness Scale for Motorcycle Couriers (OSAS-MC) to address this gap. Drawing on Türkiye’s OHS Law No. 6331, international OHS standards, and feedback from five domain experts, an initial item pool was generated and refined into a 30-item, six-dimensional instrument covering OHS Legislation Knowledge, OHS Practices, Personal Protective Equipment Use, Motorbike Use, OHS Exposure, and OHS Risk Factors. The scale was administered to 265 actively employed motorcycle couriers in Türkiye. Exploratory factor analysis supported a six-factor solution explaining 67.79% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis indicated an acceptable model fit (CFI = 0.875; RMSEA = 0.076; χ²/df = 2.543). Internal consistency was high overall (Cronbach’s α = 0.878) and across sub-dimensions (α = 0.805–0.895), and item discrimination was confirmed via upper-lower 27% group comparisons. The OSAS-MC offers a reliable, context-sensitive instrument for assessing safety awareness in high-risk, platform-mediated delivery work, and provides policymakers, platform operators, and labour organisations with a diagnostic tool to identify awareness gaps and guide targeted interventions.

items.title: Development of An English Language Learning Model Through Gamification Technology for Higher Education
items.abstract: This study investigated higher education instructors' needs regarding gamified English language learning and developed an Applied Linguistics-informed instructional model for English as a Foreign Language (EFL) instruction. Grounded in Second Language Acquisition (SLA) theory—including Gardner's (1985) motivation framework, Communicative Language Teaching (CLT) principles, and Self-Determination Theory (SDT)—the study employed an Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, and Evaluation (ADDIE)-guided Design and Development Research (DDR) approach. A purposive sample of 158 EFL instructors completed a validated 15-item questionnaire (IOC = 0.80–1.00; α = 0.81). Findings indicated strong support for gamification in promoting communicative engagement, learner autonomy, and intrinsic motivation. Based on these findings, a five-component gamification-integrated model was developed and evaluated by five experts using an 11-item instrument (α = 0.85), achieving an overall mean rating of 4.60 (very high). The study contributes to Applied Linguistics and English language education by presenting an SLA-informed model that operationalizes gamification as a structured communicative pedagogy rather than isolated game mechanics, offering an empirically informed and theoretically grounded framework for EFL instruction in Thai higher education.

items.title: Digital technologies and mental health in young people in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract: Scientific literature has shown an association between the use of digital technologies and the mental health of higher education students. However, gaps remain regarding the digital practices used to promote mental health literacy. In this context, a qualitative study was conducted using six focus groups, involving 43 students from 32 courses at 18 Portuguese higher education institutions. Thematic analysis of the data identified five themes: Digital habits; Digital technologies in mentalhealth literacy; Impact of digital technologies on well-being and mental health; Evaluation of digital technologies in mental health; Good practices in promoting well-being and mental health. The results show that the focus groups provided spaces for critical reflection and collective construction of knowledge concerning the benefits, risks and limitations of digital technologies in mental health. However, a discrepancy was identified between the participants’ critical discourse and their actualpractices. Despite reservations about the use of non-specialist digital tools, there is widespread reliance on social media content and artificial intelligence. This finding highlights a focus on immediacy, anonymity and accessibility, underscoring the need to gain a better understanding of these mechanisms and to improve access to specialist services.

items.title: DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES AND STUDENT-CENTERED LEARNING IN MODERN HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The digital transformation of education has significantly changed approaches to teaching and learning in higher education. Traditional teacher-centered instruction is increasingly being supplemented by interactive, personalized, and student-centered learning models supported by digital technologies. This article examines the pedagogical potential of learning management systems, digital communication platforms, artificial intelligence tools, multimedia resources, virtual learning environments, and online assessment technologies. The study employs theoretical analysis and synthesis of contemporary educational research. The results suggest that digital technologies can strengthen students’ autonomy, collaboration, critical thinking, motivation, and access to educational resources when they are integrated according to clearly defined pedagogical objectives. At the same time, excessive dependence on technology, digital inequality, academic integrity problems, information overload, and insufficient digital competence among educators remain important challenges. The paper argues that the effectiveness of educational digitalization depends not on the quantity of technological tools but on their pedagogically appropriate application. items.title: Digital Transformation of Disaster Response in Wajima City Following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake: Implementation Process and Operational Conditions —A Comparative Case Analysis of Five Operations—
items.abstract: This study examines the implementation process and operational conditions determining the success or failure of the digital transformation of disaster response in Wajima City, Ishikawa Prefecture, following the 2024 Noto Peninsula Earthquake. The study is based on a single-case comparative analysis of five operations—post-earthquake building safety assessment, shelter management, temporary housing, facility management, and publicly funded demolition—using operational records, products, meeting materials, and development logs. These operations were compared using five dimensions: digitalization of information collection, accumulation of shareable data, situational awareness through visualization, connection to decision support, and cross-departmental coordination. Among the five operations, post-earthquake building safety assessment and temporary housing advanced most continuously, while shelter management and facility management tended to remain at the stage of visualization, and publicly funded demolition remained fragmented. The results reveal that the digital transformation of disaster response progressed step by step from data input to accumulation, visualization, and decision support, rather than emerging all at once. Self-contained operations tended to advance more smoothly, whereas cross-departmental operations required clearer coordination and decision-making mechanisms. Thus, success depended less on technology itself than on operational conditions, implying that effective implementation depends on the peacetime preparation of data items, identifiers, update responsibilities, and decision-making arrangements.

items.title: DPMF: A Dynamic Risk-Aware Permission Framework for Securing AI Agents Using Third-Party APIs
items.abstract: AI agents are moving from systems that only generate information to systems that can plan tasks, use tools, and perform operations through external APIs. This shift creates a security problem that traditional permission models do not fully address: an agent may hold broad privileges even when a particular task needs only a small part of that access. A valid token therefore does not automatically mean that every action produced by the agent is appropriate. This paper proposes DPMF (Dynamic Risk-Aware Permission Framework), an external authorization layer for AI agents that interact with third-party services. DPMF evaluates each proposed API action using contextual signals such as user-intent alignment, data sensitivity, permission severity, source trust, action reversibility, and behavioral deviation. The resulting risk level drives one of four decisions: Allow, Restrict, Human Approval, or Deny. The framework also separates the agent's ability to propose an action from the security layer's authority to approve it. The paper presents the framework architecture, threat model, risk-scoring approach, dynamic permission algorithm, case study, and an experimental methodology for comparing DPMF with static authorization. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally implemented, no numerical performance claims are presented as established results. Instead, measurable evaluation criteria and expected outcomes are defined.

items.title: Driving the future: Evaluating a training concept for advanced driver assistance systems
items.abstract: With the widespread adoption of Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS), the need for effective ADAS driver training increases. However, empirical evidence regarding the effectiveness of ADAS education remains limited. This study evaluated the effectiveness of an ADAS driver training program across four European countries. The training included classroom-based theoretical instruction and practical hands-on experience on test-tracks and open-roads. 166 participants completed a questionnaire measuring their knowledge, attitudes, and behavioral intentions towards ADAS pre- and post-training. Overall knowledge of system purpose, handling and limitations improved significantly with the training. However, some misunderstandings remained, and in some cases, misconceptions from before the training were not corrected. Perceived safety and trust remained unchanged while willingness to use ADAS systems, and the perceived ease of use and usefulness of ADAS increased. Future training should not only provide information for trainees but also identify misconceptions they may hold. Follow-up or feedback sessions are recommended to address potential misunderstandings.

items.title: Educommunication and artificial intelligence for learning, creating, and communicating: professional competency development in university prosumers
items.abstract: Introduction This study examines the pedagogical integration of educommunication and artificial intelligence (AI) and its association with self-reported professional competencies among university prosumers-students who simultaneously consume, produce, and share academic content through digital platforms. Methods A non-experimental, cross-sectional quantitative design with descriptive-correlational and structural purposes was employed. Data were collected using a psychometrically validated 26-item Likert-scale questionnaire (plus six open-response items) administered to a convenience sample of 547 university students enrolled at Universidad Politécnica Salesiana, Ecuador. The instrument assessed five dimensions: (1) AI-mediated learning processes, (2) educommunication and expression, (3) knowledge prosumption, (4) perceived professional competencies, and (5) ethics and critical AI use. Psychometric validation confirmed excellent reliability (Cronbach's α = 0.91; McDonald's ω = 0.93). Exploratory factor analysis supported the five-factor structure (Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin [KMO] = 0.91; Bartlett's test p < 0.001; variance explained = 61.4%). Confirmatory factor analysis indicated a satisfactory model fit (comparative fit index [CFI] = 0.96; Tucker-Lewis index [TLI] = 0.95; root mean square error of approximation [RMSEA] = 0.052; standardized root mean square residual [SRMR] = 0.061). A single-factor test yielded a first unrotated factor accounting for 28.3% of the variance, below the 50% threshold, offering a preliminary indication against a single dominant method factor, although this test alone does not rule out common method bias (see Section 3.3). Results Structural equation modeling revealed significant direct paths from AI-mediated learning to perceived professional competencies ( β = 0.58, p < 0.001) and from educommunication to knowledge prosumption ( β = 0.51, p < 0.001), with knowledge prosumption partially mediating the educommunication-competency association ( β _indirect = 0.21; R² = 0.74 for D3; R² = 0.78 for D4), and ethics and critical AI use functioning as a significant moderator of the AI learning-competency path (interaction β = 0.34, p < 0.001). Given the cross-sectional, self-report design, these results are interpreted as structural associations rather than causal effects. Discussion Findings indicate that AI integration within educommunicative frameworks is positively associated with autonomous learning, creativity, and digital communication skills. However, risks associated with technological over-reliance and epistemic dependency were also identified in the qualitative data. These findings constitute structurally validated evidence that pedagogical AI integration, framed within educommunicative approaches, is associated with the perceived development of critical, collaborative, and innovative professional competencies in higher education.

items.title: Effectiveness of AI-Supported Learning in English Vocabulary Acquisition among Undergraduate Learners: A Quasi-Experimental Study
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the effectiveness of structured AI-supported learning in English vocabulary acquisition among undergraduate learners. A quasi-experimental design involved two intact B.A. Part-I student divisions at Shri Vijaysinha Yadav College, Peth Vadgaon. Both groups received instruction covering 100 target vocabulary items in four areas. The Experimental Group received teacher-guided support through an AI-Supported Vocabulary Learning Cycle using NotebookLM and ChatGPT for learning, practice, feedback, and revision. Both groups subsequently completed the same 100 item vocabulary post-test. Independent samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Cohen’s d were used. The Experimental Group achieved a significantly higher overall mean score (75.53) than the Control Group (66.95), t(70) = 6.39, p < .001, d = 1.51. All four categories showed significant differences, strongest for phrasal verbs. Gender showed no significant difference, whereas previous AI exposure and regular smartphone use were associated with higher achievement among Experimental Group learners. The findings suggest that AI can contribute to vocabulary learning when carefully and purposefully integrated with teacher-led classroom instruction and curriculum objectives. AI extends practice, feedback, revision, and application. Overall findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the intact-group design and absence of delayed assessment.

items.title: Effectiveness of occupational safety and health training in virtual reality: a comparative study with traditional methods
items.abstract: This article analyses the effectiveness and perception of occupational safety and health (OSH) training using virtual reality (VR) compared to traditional methods. The aim of the study was to verify the effectiveness of VR training compared to traditional methods (Research No. 1) and to analyse the impressions of participants with different experiences with VR in the training system (Research No. 2). Research No. 1, conducted on students in the fields of construction and occupational health and safety, compared test results after traditional training (in person / online training) and VR (the “VR training at work at height” application). Research No. 2 included active construction workers, analysing their opinions on the usefulness, engagement, and impact of VR training on hazard knowledge, using questionnaires and participant observation. Research No. 1’s results showed a significant improvement in test scores after VRtraining (an average increase of 22%), suggesting a higher effectiveness of this method. In Research No. 2, participants rated highly the usefulness of VR in health and safety training, comfort with VR devices, and their own participation. The results of the study confirm the effectiveness of VR training in occupational safety and health, increasing the effectiveness and participation of participants. Immersion, visualisation, and simulation of harsh working conditions are key advantages of this technology. The VR training system combines the experience of virtual reality with learning theory, simulating emergency response procedures and procedures for the use of personal protective equipment.

items.title: Effects of Job Satisfaction on the Performance of Employees in Various Industries
items.abstract: Job satisfaction is widely recognised as a critical determinant of employee performance, organisational productivity, and long-term institutional effectiveness across diverse economic sectors. This paper examines the relationship between job satisfaction and employee performance through a comparative lens that considers both developed and developing country contexts. Drawing on a systematic literature review of empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, the study synthesises evidence from a broad range of industries, including education, telecommunications, banking and financial services, information technology, automotive, healthcare, retail, construction, agriculture, logistics, energy, public administration, and manufacturing.The findings reveal a consistently positive and statistically significant association between job satisfaction and employee performance, either directly or through mediating mechanisms such as work engagement, organisational commitment, and motivation. Across sectors, job satisfaction is shaped by a combination of structural and motivational factors, including working conditions, training and development, leadership quality, compensation, career advancement opportunities, organisational support, and job design. Employees who report higher satisfaction levels tend to demonstrate stronger commitment, greater discretionary effort, higher productivity, and improved service quality.

items.title: ENGLISH-MAJOR STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF AI-ASSISTED IELTS WRITING TASK 2 PRACTICE IN HIGHER EDUCATION: A QUALITATIVE STUDY AT THANH DO UNIVERSITY, VIETNAM
items.abstract: This study investigated English-major students’ perceptions of AI-assisted tools in IELTS Writing Task 2 practice at Thanh Do University, Vietnam. The study aimed to explore how students perceived the usefulness and challenges of using AI-assisted writing technologies during IELTS-oriented writing activities. A qualitative research design was employed, involving semi-structured interviews with 15 third-year English-major students enrolled in the Integrated English 2 course during the second semester of the 2025 academic year. The participants had experience using AI-assisted tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Gemini to support IELTS Writing Task 2 practice. Interview data were analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings revealed that students generally perceived AI-assisted writing tools positively due to their usefulness in idea generation, essay organization, grammar correction, vocabulary enhancement, and self-study support. Participants also believed that AI technologies improved writing confidence and encouraged learner autonomy. However, concerns regarding overreliance on AI-generated content, reduced independent thinking, and the reliability of AI-generated feedback were also identified. The study highlights the potential of AI-assisted writing technologies as supplementary learning resources in IELTS-oriented writing instruction while emphasizing the importance of responsible and balanced AI integration in higher education contexts.

items.title: ENHANCING STUDENT ENGAGEMENT THROUGH AI-BASED LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS
items.abstract: This conference paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI)-based learning environments can enhance student engagement in higher education. The study focuses on the integration of learning analytics, recommendation systems, intelligent tutoring, adaptive feedback, and interactive programming tasks to support behavioral, cognitive, emotional, and social engagement. The proposed model links learner profiling, real-time analytics, personalization, feedback, and pedagogical design into a unified engagement-oriented learning environment. A model-based experimental framework is presented with sample indicators and illustrative results. The findings suggest that AI-supported adaptive learning environments may increase student participation, improve persistence in programming tasks, strengthen self-regulated learning, and support the development of programming competence. The paper also discusses implementation challenges, including data privacy, teacher readiness, infrastructure, and the need for human-centered AI design. Keywords: artificial intelligence, student engagement, AI-based learning environment, learning analytics, adaptive feedback, personalized learning

items.title: Enter the Agentomaly: How Billions of Personal AI Agents Will Become the New Economy
items.abstract: Persistent personal AI agents may change the relationship between an individual's attention and productive capacity. This paper defines Agentomaly as a proposed transition in which individuals can affordably sustain adaptive, concurrent delegated work that previously required more direct attention or organizational support. Delegation and automation are not new. The hypothesis concerns a change in their accessibility, flexibility, persistence, and coordination cost at the level of the individual principal. The paper distinguishes three questions: whether agents expand individual productive capacity; whether their interactions become a substantial operational layer of the economy; and whether the resulting systems preserve meaningful human authority. These outcomes need not coincide. A closed platform could deliver large productivity gains while concentrating control and making exit difficult. The proposed analytical unit is the principal-agent relationship. Its performance should be evaluated through quality-adjusted completed outcomes, principal attention, total human labor, elapsed time, resource cost, and externalities. More agent activity is not evidence of more economic value. The paper also develops the Principal Concentration Problem: many agent identities may represent one controlling organization rather than independent market participants. A governance framework addresses bounded mandates, audit, continuity, portability, and human re-entry. These are design commitments to assess separately from productivity, not assumed consequences of technical capability. A research agenda proposes comparisons with manual work, AI-assisted work, conventional automation, and human delegation. The 2030 horizon is a scenario boundary, not a forecast. The contribution is an integrated framework for testing when persistent delegation expands individual agency, how its benefits and costs are distributed, and whether its expansion remains subject to effective human control.

items.title: Ethical Frameworks and Guideline for the Conceptualisation and Use of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Innovations in Nursing Education and Practice: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background and rationale Digital health technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly transforming healthcare delivery, health professional education, clinical decision-making, workforce development, and health-system organisation. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises digital health as an important mechanism for strengthening health systems and improving access to equitable, efficient and high-quality healthcare (World Health Organization [WHO], 2025a), reflecting the continuing importance of digital health transformation globally (WHO, 2025b). AI has particular potential to influence clinical decision-making, service delivery, education and research. In nursing and midwifery, AI technologies have been applied across direct patient care, administration and management, and, to a lesser extent, education. A systematic review by O’Connor et al. (2023) identified 140 studies involving applications of AI to nursing and midwifery, with most applications directed towards clinical practice and patient care. However, the review also identified important limitations and risks, including poor-quality datasets and potential bias, privacy and trust concerns, the need for clinical interpretation of AI-generated results, and limited AI expertise among nurses and midwives. These findings demonstrate that implementation of AI is not solely a technological issue but also has professional, educational, ethical and governance implications. The rapid adoption of AI and other digital technologies creates opportunities to improve healthcare access, efficiency, clinical decision-making and patient outcomes, while simultaneously raising significant ethical, legal and social concerns. The WHO has emphasised that ethics and human rights should be central to the design, development, deployment and use of AI for health (WHO, 2021). Its guidance identifies principles including protecting human autonomy; promoting the public interest; ensuring transparency, explainability and intelligibility; fostering responsibility and accountability; and promoting AI that is responsive and sustainable. These principles highlight the importance of considering ethics throughout the lifecycle of health technologies rather than only after technologies have been implemented. Ethical considerations are especially important in nursing because nurses have sustained interactions with patients and families and frequently engage with health information systems, digital technologies and clinical decision-support tools at the point of care. The increasing incorporation of AI into nursing therefore raises questions concerning professional accountability, autonomy, informed consent, privacy and confidentiality, data security, algorithmic bias, transparency, equity, patient safety, trust and preservation of human-centred care (Badawy et al., 2025; Mohammed et al., 2025). Ethical issues are also emerging in nursing education as generative AI becomes increasingly accessible to students and educators. De Gagne et al. (2024) argue that the integration of AI into nursing education requires consideration of established ethical principles, including autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice and explicability. They emphasise the need for ethical principles to be incorporated into curricula and for appropriate guidance to support responsible AI use. Other nursing education literature has similarly identified potential benefits of AI and AI-enabled chatbots for personalised learning, simulation, accessibility and educator support, alongside concerns relating to privacy, confidentiality, bias and appropriate use (Srinivasan et al., 2024). Despite increasing recognition of these issues, the evidence relevant to nursing remains dispersed across different technologies, settings, populations and types of ethical consideration. Existing reviews demonstrate that ethical challenges associated with AI in nursing are substantial (Badawy et al., 2025; Mohammed et al., 2025), while broader reviews demonstrate considerable variation in how AI is being introduced and evaluated across nursing and midwifery practice (O’Connor et al., 2023). However, identifying ethical concerns alone does not establish what ethical frameworks, guidelines, principles or governance approaches are being used to guide the conceptualisation and application of these technologies, nor how such guidance is operationalised in nursing education and practice. There is therefore a need to systematically map primary research addressing the ethical conceptualisation and application of AI and digital health innovations within nursing. In particular, it is important to identify the ethical guidelines, frameworks, principles and empirically derived recommendations reported in the literature; describe their underlying characteristics and intended applications; and examine the factors associated with their implementation or application in nursing education and practice. Such mapping can clarify the current evidence base, identify areas of convergence and inconsistency, reveal gaps between ethical principles and their practical implementation, and identify priorities for future nursing research, education, professional guidance and governance. Accordingly, this scoping review aims to map how AI and digital health innovations are conceptualised and applied ethically in nursing practice and education. A scoping review is appropriate because the purpose is to examine the breadth and characteristics of the available evidence, identify the ethical frameworks and principles represented across heterogeneous primary studies, and explore factors associated with their application rather than determine the effectiveness of a single intervention. Aim: The overall aim of this scoping review is to map how artificial intelligence and digital health innovations are conceptualised and applied ethically in nursing practice and education. The review will additionally map, where reported: • the characteristics and underlying ethical principles of identified guidelines, frameworks or recommendations; • the types of AI and digital health technologies to which ethical considerations are applied; • the nursing settings and populations in which these considerations arise; • the intended or actual applications of identified ethical guidance in nursing education and clinical practice; and • barriers, facilitators and other contextual considerations associated with ethical implementation and use. items.title: Ethics, Policy, and Governance
items.abstract: Fairness is one of the fundamental ethical principles governing the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. AI systems increasingly influence learning recommendations, assessment, student support, admissions, academic advising, and institutional decision-making. Because these systems can affect educational opportunities, fairness must be considered throughout their design, development, deployment, and evaluation. An AI system is not automatically fair simply because it uses mathematical or computational methods. If the data, assumptions, objectives, or decision processes contain bias, the resulting system may reproduce or amplify existing inequalities. A simplified framework is: Educational Data → AI Model → Prediction/Recommendation → Educational Decision → Student Outcome Fairness requires examining every stage of this process. Fairness in AI-based education refers to the principle that learners should be treated equitably and should not experience unjustified disadvantage because of characteristics unrelated to legitimate educational objectives.Fairness involves: Equal opportunity Non-discrimination Appropriate treatment Inclusive access Consistent evaluation Protection from unjustified bias Fairness does not always mean treating every learner identically. Different learners may require different forms of support to achieve equitable educational opportunities. The major objectives include: Reducing discriminatory outcomes Providing equitable educational opportunities Identifying and reducing algorithmic bias Supporting inclusive learning Ensuring equitable access to AI systems Protecting vulnerable learners Promoting trustworthy educational technologies Fairness should be considered throughout: Data Collection → Model Development → Testing → Deployment → Monitoring A system that is fair during development may produce unfair outcomes after deployment if the educational environment changes. AI systems learn from data. If historical educational data contain unequal patterns, an AI system may reproduce them. For example: Historical Bias → Training Data → AI Model → Potentially Biased Prediction

items.title: EurekaBench: Measuring Agentic Ability to Discover New Scientific Insights
items.abstract: When Isaac Newton discovered the law of gravitation, he did so through an iterative process of analyzing observed data such as planetary patterns, finding the underlying mechanisms by describing patterns in mathematical equations, and refining his theory against the Moon's orbit, revealing the startling insight that the same force governs both falling apples and orbiting planets. Would it be possible for AI agents to make similar discoveries? To measure this ability, we introduce EurekaBench, a cross-domain benchmark that tests AI agents' ability to conduct long-horizon experiments and discover mechanisms that explain observations. We evaluate these mechanisms by the scientific insights that can be derived from them. EurekaBench contains an expert-verified set of 26 long-horizon tasks across neuroscience, computer science, chemistry, astrophysics, geophysics, and plasma physics, with a total of 306 scientific insights that the discovered mechanisms are expected to support. Our evaluation framework tests three axes of scientific discovery: agents' ability to follow known scientific constraints, the predictive accuracy of the discovered mechanisms, and whether these mechanisms yield scientific insights or inform future research. Our results show that current AI agents often overly fixate on predictive accuracy optimization, surpassing human scientists, while falling substantially short in deriving scientific insights.

items.title: Evaluating Agentic AI: The Multi-Layer Evaluation Model (MLE-A)
items.abstract: The emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) marks a shift from reactive educational technologies towards systems capable of autonomous multi-step planning, tool orchestration, and adaptive decision-making. As these systems contribute to structuring study pathways, generating feedback, and monitoring learner progression, elements of cognitive and metacognitive regulation become distributed between learners and AI agents. However, existing evaluation approaches in educational technology remain largely focused on usability, performance, and satisfaction, and are therefore insufficient to capture these dynamic and distributed forms of agency. This paper proposes the Multi-Layer Evaluation Model for Agentic AI (MLE-A), a conceptual framework for assessing the educational impact of agentic systems across five interacting dimensions: cognitive, metacognitive, affective, behavioural, and system-level governance. The model provides a structured basis for analysing human–AI collaboration and supporting future empirical evaluation.

items.title: Evaluating AI chatbots for providing health advice on occupational sedentary behavior in the workplace
items.abstract: Background Office workers accumulate most of their waking h in sedentary behavior, yet scalable personalized occupational-health advice remains limited, and the quality of large language model (LLM)-based tools in this domain has not been rigorously examined. Objective This study evaluated whether a domain-specialized chatbot system for providing health advice on sedentary behavior, integrating retrieval augmentation, a curated corpus, and safety guardrails, performs better than a general-purpose LLM and static educational materials. Methods A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. In the blinded expert evaluation, nine raters independently rated 60 responses across five quality dimensions. In the user survey, 654 eligible Chinese office workers interacted with the specialized chatbot and completed six perception scales (two adapted from established technology-acceptance frameworks and four developed for this study) plus open-ended feedback. Results Inter-rater reliability was good for the composite score; in a case-level safety screen, no response from the specialized chatbot or the standard materials was flagged as potentially unsafe, whereas two Doubao responses were flagged by two or more raters. The specialized chatbot achieved the highest composite rating, followed by Doubao and standard materials. In a linear mixed-effects model and crossed random intercepts for rater and question, all Holm-adjusted pairwise contrasts were significant. Advantages of the specialized chatbot over Doubao were most pronounced on safety in symptom-management and special-population items. Among users, perceived ease of use was highest, whereas perceived safety and intention to use were rated comparatively lower. Frequent prior AI-chatbot use was associated with higher ratings on all six scales; after covariate adjustment the association persisted for five of the six scales but was attenuated and no longer significant for perceived safety. Conclusion The specialized chatbot system received expert-rated accuracy and safety scores that did not differ significantly from standard educational materials, but exceeded standard materials on usefulness, comprehensibility, and completeness, and outperformed the general-purpose LLM on accuracy, safety, completeness, and the overall composite score. These findings concern response quality and immediate user perceptions, not behavioral or clinical outcomes. Nonetheless, users remained cautious about safety and intention to use after this brief exposure.

items.title: Evaluating The Impact of An Ai-Driven Clinical Decision Support System on Nursing Students' Accuracy in Care-Plan Formulation During Telemedicine Practicum
items.abstract: Care-plan formulation is among the most cognitively demanding competencies that pre-registration nursing students must master, and errors made at this formative stage may persist into qualified practice. Two contemporary developments converge on this competency: the emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) capable of suggesting nursing diagnoses and interventions, and the normalization of the telemedicine practicum as a clinical learning environment. No prior synthesis has examined their intersection. The aim of this study is to identify, appraise, and synthesize the evidence on the effect of AI-driven CDSS on the accuracy of nursing students’ care-plan formulation within telemedicine practicum settings. The review is designed and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement and conducted with reference to the Cochrane Handbook and the JBI Manual for Evidence Synthesis. Eight databases and grey-literature sources searched for peer-reviewed English-language studies published between 2015 and 2026. Screening, extraction, and appraisal were performed in duplicate; risk of bias was assessed with design-appropriate instruments (RoB 2, ROBINS-I, JBI checklists, MMAT), and certainty was rated using GRADE. Heterogeneity precluded meta-analysis, and a structured narrative synthesis following SWiM guidance was undertaken. The evidence converges on a conditional benefit. Structured, taxonomy-aligned decision support raised students’ diagnostic and care-plan accuracy relative to unsupported practice, with the inference model, the supervision arrangement, and learner characteristics acting as decisive moderators. Generative large language models produced substantial gains in rated plan quality but exhibited a characteristic failure mode of fluent yet taxonomy-discordant output, creating conditions in which automation bias is most hazardous. The telemedicine setting amplified both the potential benefit and the risk of uncritical reliance. The study concludes that an AI-driven CDSS functions as a conditional cognitive scaffold rather than an unconditional accelerator of accuracy. Its educational value in the telemedicine practicum is realized only where outputs are aligned with recognized nursing taxonomies, system reasoning is transparent, and use is embedded within supervised, deliberate practice that preserves the student as the accountable clinical reasoner. Recommendations are made for nursing education, policy, and future primary research.

items.title: Exception Exposure Deprivation and Emergency Readiness Vulnerability among Seafarers in Highly Standardized Ship Operations
items.abstract: Modern ship operations use strict procedures and advanced automation, which may reduce seafarers’ experience in handling unexpected situations. This study aims to analyze the relationship between exception exposure deprivation and emergency readiness vulnerability among seafarers. A quantitative correlational method was conducted through a questionnaire survey involving 100 seafarers and maritime trainees in Banten, Indonesia. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, validity and reliability tests, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. The results indicate that limited exposure to abnormal situations is associated with lower emergency readiness among seafarers. This study highlights the importance of realistic emergency training and varied scenarios to improve maritime safety and human performance.

items.title: Executive Judgement in AI-Mediated Decision-Making Environments: A Process Theory of Formation, Qualification Attrition and Authorisation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can contribute to the representations, alternatives and evaluations through which executive judgements are formed. Existing research already explains important aspects of hybrid cognition, reliance, managerial agency and accountability. This article develops a narrower process challenge: locally competent human and AI contributions can still culminate in an inadequately warranted organisational commitment when established operational assumptions, uncertainties or dependencies are lost or transformed before authorisation. It proposes qualification attrition as the process through which such epistemically consequential content is weakened across successive transformations, and a formation--authorisation gap as the resulting discrepancy between the grounds required for warranted commitment and those that remain accessible, intelligible and challengeable to the authorising role. Executive judgement governance is defined through four dimensions: boundary setting, interpretive challenge, reliance calibration, and authorisation with answerability. Four propositions connect transformation, qualification attrition and governance arrangements to epistemic risk, accountability risk and judgement quality. The contribution is an integrative process theory of how distributed judgement formation can fail as a composition even where individual contributions, local reliance decisions and formal accountability arrangements appear competent.

items.title: Exploring the Impact of Technological Readiness, Teaching Supports, and Peer Interaction on Cognitive Presence and Learning Outcomes in TVET-Based Smart Grid Engineering Education
items.abstract: Electronics Engineering is rapidly transforming into a sustainable digital-based system. This requires engineers to continuously strive to develop cognitive, self-regulation, and technological competencies. This study examines the influence of Technology Readiness (TR), Instructional Support (TS), and Peer Interaction (PI) on Cognitive Presence (CP) and Learning Outcomes (LO). Learning Outcomes are achieved after first going through the mediation role of Self Regulatory Learning (SRL) and Cognitive Engagement (CE) in Smart Grid Engineering Education. This study involved 120 undergraduate students. We applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4 in the data analysis. The results showed that Teaching Support significantly predicted Peer Interaction, Self-Regulatory Learning, and Technology Readiness, indicating its important role in teaching. Self-Regulatory Learning positively influenced Cognitive Engagement, which in turn strengthened Cognitive Presence and improved Learning Outcomes. However, Peer Interaction and Technology Readiness did not directly influence Cognitive Engagement, indicating that technology familiarity and collaboration alone are not enough without effective learning support. Overall, these findings validate the expanded Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework and emphasize the importance of pedagogical design in integrating sustainable technology-based learning. This study contributes to the development of adaptive, technology-based, cognitively rich environments that support sustainable engineering education.

items.title: Factores organizacionales asociados al burnout en profesionales de salud, educación y telecomunicaciones: estudio cualitativo en la Baixada Fluminense, Brasil
items.abstract: The study identifies the organizational factors that contribute to the development of burnout syndrome among professionals in the health, education, and telecommunications sectors in the Baixada Fluminense region, part of the metropolitan area of the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This is an exploratory study with a qualitative approach. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with seven professionals, and the empirical material was analyzed following Bardin’s content analysis procedures. The results indicate that factors such as work overload, micromanagement, lack of autonomy, and a high-pressure environment are determinants of emotional exhaustion, reduced productivity, and high staff turnover. Participants identified work overload and the accumulation of duties, limited autonomy, pressure related to goals and deadlines, and insufficient organizational support as the main organizational factors. Several interviewees reported difficulties disconnecting from work, interference with their personal lives, fatigue, stress, and a perceived deterioration in emotional well-being. Some also reported having considered leaving their jobs. Most participants did not identify specific organizational actions aimed at preventing burnout, although one divergent experience involving institutional emotional health initiatives was observed. It is concluded that the absence of effective organizational strategies for burnout prevention perpetuates the vulnerability of these workers, reinforcing the urgent need for more localized and effective occupational health policies.

items.title: Foundations of Artificial Intelligence in Education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence has also been closely associated with the progression from Industry 4.0 toward Industry 5.0. While Industry 4.0 emphasized automation, cyber-physical systems, and smart manufacturing, Industry 5.0 introduces a human-centred approach that balances technological innovation with creativity, ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility.
