items.title: From instructions to intelligent synthesis: conceptual art, distributed creativity, and the posthuman turn in AI-powered artistic practices
items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the groundbreaking development of AI technologies such as text-to-image generation has revealed the unprecedented potential of machines in the realm of artistic creation. This has reignited and intensified widespread reflections on historical issues in artistic practice, including ontological questions, the identity of the author, the configuration of human–machine relationships, and the positioning of creativity. To address these concerns, this paper mainly seeks to draw inspiration from the important artistic thoughts of two conceptual artists who were active in the 1960s: Yoko Ono and Sol LeWitt. It also explores the interconnectedness and continuity between generative AI art practices and the legacy of conceptual art, tracing the historical trajectory of the relationship between conceptual art and digital art. Beyond the pivotal artistic practices of these two pioneering conceptual artists, the comparative analysis also encompasses the examination of additional associated artistic endeavors in relation to text-guided image synthesis. This broader scope of artists aims to more comprehensively support the argument on the impact of artificial intelligence on participatory frameworks and the concept of authorship within future creative practices. By delving into a discussion on dematerialization with conceptual art’s focus on concepts over material objects, the authors explore the potential for a posthumanist paradigm in AI art practices, to consider the reconfiguration of creativity in human–machine collaborations. Through speculative explorations of AI visualizations of Ono's and LeWitt's instructions and evaluating the role of "prompt engineering" in collaborative creation, new forms of distributed creativity that respond to posthumanist provocations are discovered. Leveraging the posthumanist emphasis on the “biological and microbiological entanglement with nonhumans”, this approach aids in dislodging the centrality of the individual or the artist within the creative process (Herbrechter 2023, p. 8). This critical examination highlights the disruptive potential of conceptual art in reshaping the notion of authorship within its symbiotic relationship with technological culture. It reveals the dynamic and co-evolutionary relationship between the conceptual art discourse and its reinterpretation within the emerging computational participatory structures of the artistic frontier. By drawing on the legacy of conceptual art, this study attempts to reconcile the tensions between conceptual completion, technological participation, artistic ontology, and distributed creativity, providing theoretical support for current AI art practices and driving the ongoing reconsideration of posthuman creative partnerships in technology mediated artistic production.

items.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science
items.abstract: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.

items.title: From Ratings to Sensors: Real-Time AIIoT-Based Credibility Anchored on Blockchain for Ride-Sharing Ecosystems
items.abstract: Current ride-sharing platforms predominantly rely on subjective post-ride ratings to evaluate driver credibility, making reputation systems vulnerable to user bias, delayed feedback, collusion, and manipulation. Although recent studies have explored blockchain-based ride-sharing, AI-driven driver monitoring, and IoT-enabled transportation independently, they do not provide an integrated trust framework that continuously derives credibility from objectively verifiable driving behaviour while maintaining scalability and low operational cost.This paper presents Ridezy, a decentralized trust architecture that replaces conventional rating-based reputation with real-time sensor-driven credibility. The proposed framework combines edge Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIIoT) technologies to continuously monitor behavioural indicators such as lane discipline, speed compliance, braking behaviour, and traffic sign adherence. Instead of storing high-frequency telemetry on the blockchain, Ridezy employs a hybrid architecture in which behavioural summaries are processed off-chain and only cryptographic hashes, credibility updates, and payment records are anchored on Polygon smart contracts, enabling tamper-evident trust with minimal blockchain overhead. To evaluate the proposed architecture, Ridezy is compared against three representative trust models: a traditional rating-based system, an AI-only architecture, and a blockchain-only architecture. The evaluation considers behavioural detection performance, end-to-end latency, cost efficiency, throughput, reputation stability, tamper resistance, and component-wise ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid architecture achieves higher behavioural fidelity and stronger trust guarantees than conventional reputation mechanisms while maintaining low per-ride blockchain cost and scalable operation through batched on-chain commitments.The primary contribution of this work is a sensor-driven credibility framework that transforms real-time behavioural evidence into a cryptographically verifiable trust primitive for ride-sharing ecosystems. By combining edge AI, IoT telemetry, and blockchain-based trust anchoring within a scalable hybrid architecture, Ridezy provides a practical foundation for trustworthy, transparent, and next-generation intelligent mobility systems.

items.title: From Structural Empowerment to Performance: A Sequential Mediation Model of Job-Design Empowerment, Psychological Empowerment, and Managerial Motivation among Bank Managers in a Developing Economy
items.abstract: Purpose: In an era of intense competition and rapid organizational change, perceived empowerment has become a critical lever for improving employee behavior and firm-level outcomes. This study examines how three empowerment approaches—perceived structural empowerment, perceived job design empowerment, and psychological empowerment—shape the task performance, contextual performance, and organizational commitment of middle-level managers in Pakistan's public and private commercial banks. Intrinsic motivation is modeled as a mediator and extrovert personality as a moderator of these relationships. Design/Methodology/Approach: Survey data were collected from 900 managers using convenience sampling, yielding 814 usable responses; data were analyzed with SPSS and AMOS using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling. Findings: Results show that perceived structural empowerment and perceived job design empowerment significantly and positively predict task performance, contextual performance, and organizational commitment, and that psychological empowerment partially mediates the effects of both forms of empowerment on these outcomes. Intrinsic motivation further mediates the relationship between psychological empowerment and the performance behaviors, while extrovert personality moderates the psychological empowerment–task performance and psychological empowerment–organizational commitment relationships but not the psychological empowerment–contextual performance relationship. Implications/Originality/Value: The findings offer banks an empowerment-based motivational framework for human resource policy that can strengthen employee performance and organizational commitment simultaneously.

items.title: Future Trends
items.abstract: AI is rapidly transforming the educational landscape, and its future impact is expected to extend beyond individual learning tools toward broader changes in teaching, assessment, institutional management, research, and educational ecosystems. Future developments may create increasingly intelligent and personalized learning environments in which humans and AI systems work together to support educational goals. The year 2035 represents an important horizon for considering the future development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education. By this period, AI may become deeply integrated into learning platforms, educational administration, research environments, assessment systems, digital classrooms, and professional education. The future of education is unlikely to be based on AI alone. Instead, educational environments may increasingly combine AI capabilities with human expertise, creativity, emotional intelligence, critical thinking, and ethical responsibility. A possible framework is: AI Technology + Human Expertise + Digital Infrastructure + Ethical Governance = Future Education By 2035, AI may become a regular component of educational environments rather than an additional technological tool. Students may interact with intelligent learning systems that continuously adapt to their learning progress, interests, abilities, and educational goals. Teachers may use AI to support lesson planning, assessment, learning analytics, content development, and personalized instruction.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI ADOPTION BY SMES: DRIVERS, BARRIERS AND PERFORMANCE OUTCOMES IN NIGERIA
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is creating new opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to improve business processes, innovation, productivity, and competitiveness. However, the factors encouraging or limiting Generative AI adoption and its performance outcomes among SMEs in Nigeria remain underexplored. This study examines Generative AI adoption by SMEs in Nigeria, focusing on its drivers, barriers, and performance outcomes. A cross-sectional survey research design was employed, with data collected from 200 SME owners, managers, and employees using a structured questionnaire titled Generative AI Adoption and SME Performance Questionnaire (GAIA-SPQ), validated with a reliability coefficient of 0.86. Data were analyzed using correlation analysis at a 0.05 level of significance. Findings reveal that drivers of Generative AI significantly influence its adoption, while barriers also significantly affect adoption negatively. The study further finds that Generative AI use significantly affects SME performance, particularly in relation to productivity and innovation. The study concludes that Generative AI provides important opportunities for improving SME performance, although effective adoption requires favourable conditions and the reduction of implementation barriers. It is recommended that SMEs strengthen their technological capabilities, develop relevant digital skills, and adopt cost-effective Generative AI solutions to improve productivity, innovation, and competitiveness.

items.title: Generative AI in Islamic Education: A Maqāṣid-Based Framework for Curriculum, Assessment and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered Islamic schools, seminaries and universities faster than the institutions can govern it. Students use chatbots to explain verses, draft essays and prepare for examinations, while teachers lack shared rules on what is permitted, how to disclose it and how to assess learning fairly. This paper proposes a practical framework that grounds those decisions in the objectives of the Sharia (maqāṣid al-sharīʿa) rather than in generic ethics alone. Using an analytical synthesis of recent evidence on generative AI in education, research on assessment and academic integrity, international governance guidance, and the maqāṣid literature, the paper maps the five classical necessities (religion, life, intellect, lineage and property) onto the risks of AI-mediated learning and derives design principles for three layers: curriculum, assessment and academic integrity. The framework calls for AI literacy grounded in the ethic of verification, assessment built on authentic and oral demonstration of understanding instead of unreliable detection software, a three-tier policy on permitted use with disclosure, and governance that protects learner data and religious content. A phased implementation route and indicators are offered for institutions. The paper is conceptual and untested in practice; it closes with a research agenda for piloting the framework, comparing it across legal schools and measuring its effects on learning.

items.title: Generative AI-Assisted Competitive Microlearning Strategy: Development and Validation of the Plomp Model in Classroom Teacher Education in Finland
items.abstract: Background. The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education has created challenges in designing responsible and adaptive learning strategies. Meanwhile, competitive elements in gamified learning remain debated due to inconsistent effects on learner engagement. Purpose. This research aimed to develop and evaluate a generative AI-assisted competitive microlearning strategy for improving instructional media development skills among Finnish Luokanopettajakoulutus (Class Teacher Education) students. Novelty. This study introduces a novel instructional design that integrates generative AI, microlearning, and optional quality-based competition. Unlike conventional competitive gamification approaches, the proposed strategy recognizes learner differences by examining whether competition produces varied outcomes across learning groups Method. Using the Plomp development model, the study involved 79 undergraduate students from four parallel classes. Data from expert validation, practicality questionnaires, and product assessments were analyzed using Aiken’s V and descriptive statistics. Results. The strategy achieved high validity (Aiken’s V = 0.87) and strong practicality (83.1% student response; 85.9% lecturer response). Variation in competition participation (41–62%) indicated different effects among learner groups. Conclusion. The findings contribute an adaptive AI-assisted microlearning framework that balances innovation, learner diversity, and educational equity in teacher education.

items.title: H-VALIDA: A Hybrid Methodological Framework for Transparent AI-Assisted Surveys in Data-Scarce Contexts: A Conceptual Framework for Responsible AI Integration
items.abstract: Survey research has taken up artificial intelligence quickly, largely because of speed, scale, and lower cost. Those same gains bring methodological risks that become especially serious where data are thin, several languages are in use, or cultural meaning is tightly layered. This article puts forward H-VALIDA (Hybrid Validation and Auditing for Localized, Interpretable, Documented, and Accountable AI-Assisted Surveys) as both a conceptual and an operational framework for AI-assisted surveys that are more reliable, more sensitive to context, and more firmly grounded in ethics. The framework draws together critical data studies, human-centred AI, the total survey error tradition, classical survey methodology, and decolonial principles of data governance. Seven interlocking pillars organise the work: Hybrid Human-AI Collaboration, Contextual Sampling, Algorithmic Auditing, Human Validation, Source Triangulation, Open Documentation, and Ethical Accountability. Those pillars are mapped onto an expanded total survey error taxonomy, and the CARE Principles for Indigenous data governance run through the design as a whole. The article is a methodological design study rather than a field experiment. Development of the framework followed a five-stage protocol: a diagnostic review of documented weaknesses in AI-assisted surveys; a structured synthesis of the literature; integration of principles; construction of the pillars; and operationalisation. Prospective appraisal rested on a specified heuristic rubric, a worked multilingual scenario, and a comparison with a purely automated baseline. No expert-panel scores, statistical tests, or national field implementation are reported here. Claims of improvement are therefore stated as theoretically grounded and operationally specified propositions that still require empirical confirmation. The central argument is that AI systems function as sociotechnical arrangements rather than as neutral instruments, and that validity depends on continuous human oversight, an open record of process, and deliberate adjustment to local conditions.

items.abstract: How can artificial intelligence (AI) best support human problem-solving, creativity, and group work? I introduce a psychological account of narrative agency that formalizes how human groups learn from, communicate, and influence narratives in digital contexts. I then discuss how AI models impact human performance through a narrative agency lens, from authoring better essays to finding consensus online. Crucially, AI outputs are routed through a human's narrative agency to generate a result that causes change in the world. Designing human–AI systems around maintaining people's narrative agency is therefore essential for human–AI alignment.

items.title: How Bridging and Bonding Social Capital Shapes Performance Expectancy of Digital Transformation Among Immigrants and Natives
items.abstract: Performance expectancy, individuals’ beliefs about the usefulness of digital transformation, could impact individuals’ intention, use, and satisfaction with technologies, yet remains an understudied topic among immigrant populations. Drawing on social capital theory, we examine how bonding and bridging social capital shape performance expectancy across different domains of digital transformation and whether these associations differ by nativity status. Using the 2022 Digital Divide Survey (N = 8,400; 7,000 native South Koreans, 700 marriage immigrants, 700 North Korean migrants), regression analyses showed that bridging social capital had positive associations with performance expectancy (b ranging from 0.43 to 0.62, p < 0.001), whereas bonding social capital was negative, particularly for networking (b = −0.09, p < 0.001) and remote work/learning (b = −0.08, p < 0.001). North Korean migrants reported the highest adjusted means of performance expectancy across all domains. Results highlight that diverse social networks generate greater perceived benefits from digital transformation.

items.title: How do humans infer silent reliability degradation in automated decision aids? A computational modelling study of first failure reports
items.abstract: Automated decision aids may undergo silent reliability degradation, in which performance declines without explicit warnings, confidence cues, or reliability-state feedback. In such situations, humans must infer whether automation has degraded from sequences of correct and incorrect outputs. This study examined the computational mechanisms underlying first failure reports in an industrial visual inspection task. We conceptualized silent-failure perception as a training-baseline-referenced first-report problem and compared five candidate mechanisms within a shared discrete-time hazard framework: Bayesian reliability learning, Delta-rule learning, CUSUM cumulative-deviation inference, recent-window heuristic monitoring, and a no-learning/reporting-tendency baseline. Trial-level data from 60 participants were analysed across three levels of failure severity and two levels of initial reliability, yielding 720 participant-scenario observations with first-report times or right-censored outcomes. PSIS-LOO model comparison showed that the Delta-rule learning model provided the strongest predictive account overall and across all reliability conditions. Posterior predictive checks further indicated that this model reproduced the cumulative time course of first failure reports. The results suggest that humans infer silent reliability degradation by tracking a current error-state estimate relative to the training baseline: errors increase this estimate, correct feedback suppresses it, and first reports become more likely when the current state shows sufficient baseline-relative deviation. Failure severity primarily shaped the density and persistence of degradation evidence, whereas initial reliability shaped the experiential baseline against which later errors were interpreted. These findings provide a mechanistic account of silent-failure perception and inform the design of reliability-transparent automated systems.

items.title: How do virtual exercise technology and social presence influence motivation to exercise?
items.abstract: Introduction Virtual technology offers a promising tool for encouraging engagement in exercise, as it can provide the user with enhanced visual stimuli and accessible metrics; however, the specific features within that technology that contribute to motivation and participation require further investigation. This study examined how different visual displays and the presence of a second rider influenced motivation to exercise using virtual technology. Methods Twenty-four young adults completed a 3-km cycling course on the same virtual track under three counterbalanced conditions including (a) a metrics-only ride, where a screen in front of the rider displayed only standard performance variables (e.g., power, cadence), (b) a solo-virtual ride, which was identical to the previous condition, but with the addition of the participant being depicted on the screen as an avatar amongst virtual scenery, and (c) a paired-virtual ride, that contained the same elements as the previous two conditions, but with the addition of a second rider represented on the screen as an avatar. Results The quantitative results, which included performance-related variables (cadence, power, speed, and heart rate), measures of intrinsic motivation, and ratings of perceived exertion, revealed significantly higher values for the paired-virtual condition compared to both the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions. Differences between the metrics-only and the solo-virtual conditions were isolated to interest-enjoyment and effort-importance. Brief interviews with participants indicated that the paired-virtual condition produced heightened levels of enjoyment and competitive drive which motivated participants to exert more effort. The solo-virtual condition was reported to be relaxing, but it was also reported as the least engaging. The metrics-only condition provoked negative emotions due to the absence of distractions and a heightened focus on internal cues. Discussion The results highlight the psychological mechanisms that influence motivation and engagement when using virtual exercise technology.

items.title: How, Not How Much? Exploring Help-Seeking Orientation and Academic Engagement in Student AI Use
items.abstract: Research often operationalizes AI use in terms of frequency; however, frequency alone does not capture why or how students use AI. Drawing on help-seeking theory, we examined whether instrumental (learning-oriented) versus executive (task-completion) orientation toward AI differentiates students in ways that frequency does not, using a survey of 107 undergraduates. Academic self-efficacy mediated the academic engagement-AI literacy association, with cognitive engagement showing the strongest engagement-literacy link. AI use frequency was negatively associated with academic engagement; this relationship remained negative and was larger in magnitude when controlling for AI literacy. Instrumental users showed higher academic engagement than executive users, despite no difference in usage frequency. These findings suggest that whether AI is treated as a thinking partner or an answer source may be more meaningful than exposure frequency alone. Implications are discussed for how educators and course designers assess and support learning-oriented AI use, including distance and online learning contexts, where self-regulated AI use is particularly consequential.

items.title: Human Factor Contributions to Accidents and Fatalities in U.S. Construction: A Comparative Analysis of Three Major Subsectors
items.abstract: Human factors remain a leading cause of occupational accidents and fatalities in the construction industry. Although human factors are a major contributor to construction accidents, their relative impact across different construction subsectors has not been fully quantified. This study presents a comparative analysis of accident and fatality data from the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) for three major construction subsectors, NAICS 236 (Construction of Buildings), 237 (Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction), and 238 (Specialty Trade Contractors) from January 2010 through June 2025. Seventy human-factor-related keywords were categorized into eight categories, and accident counts, fatality counts, and fatality rates, defined as the proportion of investigated cases that were fatal, were computed. Twenty-four high-frequency keywords (≥60 investigated accidents) were further analyzed across the three subsectors. Descriptive methods, including risk matrices, Pareto analysis, and category-level fatality rate comparisons, were applied to identify the factors contributing most to fatalities. Differences between subsectors were tested using permutation-based chi-square tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple comparisons. Results indicate substantial variation in both frequency and severity among keywords. At the category level, cognitive or perceptual errors, procedural violations and unsafe acts, and judgment and awareness failures in equipment use showed significantly higher fatality proportions in Heavy and Civil Engineering Construction than in the other two subsectors, whereas at the keyword level only lost balance and inattention differed significantly once the correction was applied. The findings provide a data-driven basis for prioritizing targeted safety interventions and tailoring human factor mitigation strategies to subsector-specific risks.

items.title: Human-Centered AI Education for Viksit Bharat @2047: Reimagining Teachers, Learners and Future-Ready Schools
items.abstract: Abstract: Artificial Intelligence is reshaping how societies function, communicate, learn and innovate, and India stands at a particularly consequential point in this shift. The arrival of generative AI, adaptive learning platforms and intelligent digital tools presents the country with both a rare opportunity and a demanding policy challenge on its path toward Viksit Bharat @2047. Education sits at the heart of this challenge, because the citizens, workers and innovators who will carry that vision forward are being shaped right now, inside today's classrooms. This conceptual paper asks how Artificial Intelligence can genuinely strengthen India's education system without eroding the human qualities that make learning meaningful: agency, creativity, ethics and social responsibility. Drawing on an integrative reading of policy documents and international literature - UNESCO's AI competency frameworks, OECD perspectives on AI literacy, India's National Education Policy 2020, the IndiaAI Mission, the World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025, ILO research on generative AI and employment, and the author's own practitioner book AI and Us - the paper argues that the real question is not whether AI will replace teachers, but whether schools can build a working partnership between teachers, learners and AI. The paper introduces a Human-Centered AI Education Framework built around six interlocking dimensions: AI Literacy, AI-Augmented Pedagogy, Human Skills, Ethical and Responsible Use, Inclusive Digital Infrastructure, and Continuous Professional Learning. It also sketches a Teacher-AI-Student ecosystem in which AI takes on assistive and analytical work while teachers hold on to pedagogical, relational and ethical authority. Viksit Bharat @2047, the paper contends, does not just need citizens who are skilled at using AI - it needs citizens who are AI-literate, critical, creative, ethical and socially engaged. The paper closes with policy recommendations aimed at schools, teacher-education institutions, government bodies and educational technology developers.

items.title: Human-Centered AI in Practice: Peer Facilitators as Technostress Reducers in a Mixed-Methods LMS Study
items.abstract: Purpose: While the rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant pedagogical potential, it often outpaces the psychological scaffolding that anxious learners require, creating a severe affective barrier known as technostress. To address this critical gap, this study investigates whether structured peer facilitation, embedded within a Learning Management System (LMS) based AI course, can effectively reduce undergraduate students' AI anxiety and strengthen their conceptual understanding. Methods/Study design/approach: An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was conducted involving 33 undergraduate students encountering generative AI instruction for the first time. Quantitative data encompassing AI anxiety, conceptual understanding, an)d technical self-efficacy were collected pre- and post-intervention, followed by analysis using Wilcoxon signed-rank tests and Spearman's rank correlation. Subsequently, qualitative data from open-ended evaluations were examined through reflexive thematic analysis to contextualize and deeply explain the quantitative shifts. Result/Findings: The intervention yielded a statistically significant reduction in AI anxiety (Z = -2.151, p = .032) alongside a significant improvement in conceptual understanding (Z = -1.990, p = .047). Although technical self-efficacy and career projection improved, the changes did not reach statistical significance. Furthermore, facilitator evaluation exhibited a significant negative correlation with anxiety reduction (rs = -.389). Thematic analysis confirmed that peer facilitators effectively acted as technical translators and technostress reducers, establishing the psychological safety necessary for learning. Novelty/Originality/Value: This research uniquely repositions peer mediation as the vital affective "more capable other" within Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development, prioritizing the resolution of emotional barriers before cognitive engagement with AI tools. The study extends Human-Centered AI (HCAI) theory by delivering robust empirical evidence that pairing generative AI modules with human peer facilitation creates a synergistic learning ecosystem. This provides educators with a scalable, practical solution for mitigating technostress in modern digital education.

items.title: Human-Centred AI for Sustainable Digital Governance in India: A Review of Digital Public Services.
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to improve public service delivery through automation, data analysis, decision support and digital interaction. In India, Digital India, Digital Public Infrastructure and national AI initiatives have created opportunities to make government services more efficient, accessible and responsive. At the same time, AI-enabled public services raise concerns related to privacy, transparency, bias, accessibility, accountability and citizen trust. This paper examines how a Human-Centred AI (HCAI) approach can support sustainable digital governance in India through a structured review of secondary literature. Recent peer-reviewed studies, government reports and institutional publications are examined using thematic analysis. The review focuses on citizen-centric service delivery, accessibility and inclusion, transparency and explainability, privacy and security, fairness, citizen trust, and human oversight. The findings indicate that AI can support intelligent service discovery, conversational assistance, multilingual interaction, personalisation and routine administrative processing. However, technological capability alone does not guarantee better public services. AI must be designed around citizen needs and supported by appropriate governance safeguards. Based on the synthesis, the paper proposes a conceptual Human-Centred AI Framework with five interconnected dimensions: human needs, inclusive digital experience, responsible AI, accountable governance and sustainable public value. The paper concludes that India's AI-enabled digital governance should balance technological innovation with accessibility, privacy, fairness, transparency, human oversight and public trust.

items.title: Human-Centred Psychological Support in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Prospects for Employee Well-Being and Organizational Trust
items.abstract: Psychological support in corporations has traditionally relied on interpersonal mechanisms, including manager support, employee assistance programmes, counselling, stress-management interventions, and occupational health services. The diffusion of artificial intelligence is changing not only the instruments used to support employees, but also the psychological architecture of support itself. This study examines how corporate psychological support has evolved from predominantly human-centred models to hybrid systems that incorporate artificial intelligence, with particular attention to psychological safety, trust, autonomy, perceived organizational support, emotional disclosure, stress, burnout, and surveillance-related anxiety. An integrative conceptual review and comparative synthesis were conducted using established theories of occupational psychology and recent evidence on workplace mental health, digital mental-health interventions, conversational agents, technostress, and AI-enabled management. The analysis applies the Job Demands-Resources model, psychological safety theory, and perceived organizational support as complementary explanatory lenses. The study identifies a transition from reactive and episodic support toward preventive, continuous, and increasingly personalized support. AI can strengthen psychological resources by improving accessibility, low-threshold help-seeking, personalization, and early identification of distress. However, the same technologies can become psychological demands when employees experience monitoring as surveillance, data collection as loss of privacy, automated recommendations as reduced autonomy, or simulated empathy as depersonalized care. AI does not inherently improve or deteriorate employee well-being. Its psychological effect depends on whether it is embedded in a human-centred support system that preserves confidentiality, voluntary participation, meaningful human contact, and professional accountability. Future studies should test the proposed dual-path model across occupations and cultures and examine how human oversight, perceived organizational motives, and AI literacy moderate the relationship between AI-mediated support and employee psychological outcomes.

items.title: Human-inspired Route Selection for Efficient Social Robot Navigation in Narrow Spaces
items.abstract: Narrow human environments are challenging for social robot navigation, where distance-optimal shortcut routes to destination are frequently blocked by people in the aisles. People in these situations select the appropriate route between detour and shortcut in an efficient and socially-aware way, by balancing their extra effort (if choosing detour) and the required effort from the person on the way to make space to pass. Similar balance strategy is utilized when people decide the politeness of the request utterance to compensate for the way yielding effort from others. Inspired by this human balance strategy, we developed a decision-making methodological framework for socially-aware high-level path planning and interaction utterance when the robot navigates in narrow shared spaces and implemented it onto a humanoid mobile robot. In order to demonstrate the transparency and utility of this framework, we present a specific instantiation by conducting a set of human-robot experiments in a real store. Data from 30 people were collected via two field experiments to identify socially-acceptable parameters. Results of a within-participants study with 28 human customers interestingly demonstrated that the proposed socially-aware method was more time-efficient compared to the detour-only and shortcut-only strategies.

items.title: Impact of AI-Enabled Features in Faculty Teaching Effectiveness in Google Classroom
items.abstract: Abstract The Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into education is transforming traditional teaching and learning practices. Google Classroom, currently with AI-enabled features such as lesson-plan generation, quiz creation, rubric development, differentiated learning resources, and suggested feedback, provides faculty with special power to improve teaching efficiency and classroom management. This study examines the impact of AI-enabled features on faculty teaching effectiveness in Google Classroom. The study mainly focuses on how AI influences lesson planning, preparation time, assessment, feedback, personalization of learning, student engagement, and overall teaching effectiveness. The study can be conducted using a structured questionnaire among faculty members who use Google Classroom. The findings are expected to show that AI can reduce routine workload and support more efficient and personalized teaching. However, factors such as AI literacy, training, accuracy of AI-generated content, privacy concerns, and the need for human supervision may influence its effectiveness. Research on AI in education also emphasizes the importance of teacher professional development and responsible implementation.

items.title: Impact of Generative AI on Formal Writing Skills of Undergraduate students
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has significantly influenced students' approach to formal writing. The present research, titled “Impact of Generative AI on the Formal Writing Practices of Undergraduate Students,” tries to examine the extent, frequency, purposes, and perceived effects of Generative AI used by undergraduate students in formal writing. A descriptive survey research design along with a quantitative approach was applied. A structured online questionnaire was prepared using Google Forms to collect primary data from undergraduate students representing programmes such as B.A., BMS, BAF, B.Com., B.Sc. Computer Science, B.Sc. IT, Psychology, History, and B.A.M.M.C. A total of 108 responses were obtained. items.title: Indirect associations involving four work-motivation dimensions between perceived organizational climate and work engagement among geriatric nursing assistants in China: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Population ageing has increased demand for long-term care, yet evidence on organizational and motivational correlates of work engagement among geriatric nursing assistants in China remains limited. Using convenience sampling, this cross-sectional survey recruited geriatric nursing assistants from nine aged care institutions in Xi’an and Weinan, Shaanxi Province, China, between May and August 2025. Of 396 returned questionnaires, 330 were included after prespecified data screening. Participants completed measures of perceived organizational climate, four work-motivation dimensions, and work engagement. Pearson correlations, observed-score regressions, four separate structural equation models, and 5,000-resample bias-corrected bootstrap analyses were conducted. Institution- and covariate-adjusted sensitivity analyses were also performed. In the joint regression model, intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.420, p < 0.001) and introjected regulation ( β = 0.324, p < 0.001) were independently associated with work engagement, whereas perceived organizational climate, identified regulation, and external regulation were not. Across the four structural equation models, perceived organizational climate was positively associated with each motivation dimension (standardized β = 0.652–0.704), and each motivation dimension was positively associated with work engagement ( β = 0.543–0.771). Because each model included only one motivation dimension, the indirect estimates were model-specific rather than unique contributions independent of the other dimensions. Significant indirect associations were observed through intrinsic motivation ( β = 0.519, bias-corrected 95% CI [0.430, 0.636]), identified regulation ( β = 0.430, [0.349, 0.532]), introjected regulation ( β = 0.530, [0.439, 0.648]), and external regulation ( β = 0.359, [0.258, 0.497]). In separate sensitivity analyses based on standardized observed scores, the four indirect associations remained statistically significant after adjustment for institutions and selected individual-level covariates. Perceived organizational climate and the four work-motivation dimensions were associated with work engagement among geriatric nursing assistants. The findings support further investigation of how organizational conditions and qualitatively different forms of work motivation relate to engagement. Because all variables were measured concurrently, temporal ordering and causal mediation cannot be established.

items.title: Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Higher Education Courses: A Maturity-Based Approach Using EMBED+
items.abstract: Digital transformation has become a strategic priority for higher education institutions (HEIs), with blended learning environments (BLEs) increasingly positioned as sustainable approaches that combine online and face-to-face learning. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering these environments, offering opportunities for personalised guidance, adaptive learning support, automated feedback, and enhanced media design. However, AI adoption often remains fragmented and technology-driven, creating challenges related to pedagogical coherence, ethics, equity, and sustainability. This paper argues that AI integration in blended courses should be understood as a maturity process rather than as a question of technology adoption alone. Using the European Maturity Model for Blended Education Plus (EMBED+) as an analytical framework, this study explores how AI-supported practices can evolve across maturity stages. The analysis focuses on two course-level dimensions where AI has particular relevance: Blended Learner Guidance and Use of Media and Tools. Through a conceptual mapping approach, AI applications are aligned with four maturity stages: ad hoc, deliberate, responsive, and embedded. Findings indicate that mature AI integration is characterised not by advanced technologies, but by intentional pedagogical design, evidence-informed improvement, and adaptive deployment. The proposed framework provides educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders with a shared language to evaluate and strengthen AI-enhanced blended learning practices.

items.abstract: The article critically analyzes and scientifically substantiates the paradigm of integrating modern information and communication technologies (ICT) and artificial intelligence (AI) tools into the system of heuristic foreign language teaching in higher education. The author demonstrates that the synergy of digital tools and generative AI serves as a powerful intensifier of the educational process, ensuring deep individualization, differentiation of learning, enhancement of students’ intrinsic motivation, and the development of their cognitive and creative autonomy. The study synthesizes practical experience in utilizing the digital ecosystem of Sumy State Pedagogical University named after A.S. Makarenko in combination with video conferencing services (Google Meet, Zoom) and adaptive AI technologies to organize flexible online learning. Particular attention is paid to the effectiveness of these tools under crisis conditions (the COVID-19 pandemic and martial law) both for the routine automation of assessment and for modeling open-ended creative tasks of an exploratory nature. The paper presents original methodological developments, including the electronic manual «Communicative Culture of Medical Students in Use», integrated with modern digital resources. Specific examples demonstrate how the use of ICT and AI assistants enables students to complete a full heuristic cycle: from analytical information processing to the generation, self-correction, and defense of their own original educational product. The author summarizes the undeniable advantages of the updated innovative higher education space, which transforms traditional subject-subject relations into a format of interactive partnership: “teacher – student – artificial intelligence”.

items.title: Intention to Adopt Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: Insights from Health Science Students through the Technology Acceptance Model
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate health science students’ intentions to adopt artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare and to identify key predictors of these intentions using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 967 students enrolled in various health-related disciplines at a university. Data were collected through a self-administered online questionnaire comprising five sections: demographic information, information technology (IT) skills, perceptions of AI in medicine, attitudes towards AI and intentions to adopt AI in healthcare. Approximately half of the participants reported high intentions to integrate AI into their future medical practice. Linear regression analyses confirmed the applicability of the TAM in predicting AI adoption intentions and identified the following three significant predictors: attitudes towards AI, perceptions of AI in medicine and IT skills. Among these, attitudes towards AI emerged as the strongest predictor (β = 0.563, t = 17.687, p < 0.001). These findings underscore the importance of fostering students’ IT competencies and positive perceptions and attitudes to facilitate the effective integration of AI into medical education and practice. Future research should employ longitudinal designs to examine changes in students’ perceptions and attitudes over time, thereby providing insights for curriculum development that better aligns with students’ evolving learning needs and ensures professional readiness.

items.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Motivation in Science Learning Among Grade 3 Pupils
items.abstract: Motivation is crucial in enhancing pupils’ interest, engagement, and positive experiences in science education. This study employed a descriptive quantitative research design to examine the intrinsic and extrinsic motivation of Grade 3 pupils in selected elementary schools in the Santa Fe District, Nueva Vizcaya. Intrinsic motivation was evaluated based on interest in science, curiosity, desire to learn, enjoyment of science activities, and self-confidence. Extrinsic motivation factors included teacher support and encouragement, rewards and recognition, classroom environment, and availability of learning materials. The research also identified obstacles impacting pupils’ motivation to learn science. Data were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire and analyzed using frequency, percentage, mean, and standard deviation (SD). The findings provide a foundation for identifying motivational strengths and areas needing further support in science education. These results underscore the importance of creating engaging classroom experiences, providing appropriate learning resources, strengthening teacher support, and maintaining a positive learning environment that encourages active participation in science activities. Based on the identified motivational needs and obstacles, a motivation-based intervention program was proposed to enhance pupils’ intrinsic and extrinsic motivation and support meaningful science learning. The findings may offer teachers and school administrators practical guidance in developing learning experiences that foster pupils’ interest, curiosity, enjoyment, confidence, and sustained engagement in science.

items.title: Introducing the LISA Framework: Level and Integration Scope of Artificial Intelligence in Learning Design (Presentation at ICL 2026, Cologne, 09/2026)
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming learning design, yet current terminology often lacks the precision to distinguish between varying levels of AI involvement. Terms like "AI-supported" obscure critical differences in decision-making authority and adaptation dynamism. This presentation introduces the LISA Framework (Level of autonomy and Interaction Scope of AI in learning design), developed within the Erasmus+ project DigiSET. LISA proposes a two-dimensional typology based on (1) the Level of AI Autonomy (human-led assistance to fully autonomous operation) and (2) the Interaction Scope (static, rule-based execution vs. dynamic, comprehensive adaptation). Six archetypes emerge: the Content Generator, the Co-Creator, the Rule-Based Agent, the Smart Assistant, the Adaptive Partner, and the Autonomous Agent. Grounded in practical experiences from Graz University of Technology, this heuristic model provides educators, researchers, and policymakers with a structured vocabulary to analyze, discuss, and strategically plan AI-enhanced learning resources. This paper was presented by Benedikt Brünner. Citation: Schön, S., Brünner, B.& Ebner, M. (2026, September 30). Professional activity, as an essential component of human life, significantly influences emotional state, stress resilience, and overall psychological stability. The results show that a healthy work environment enhances psychological stability and life satisfaction.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of artificial intelligence anxiety among undergraduate nursing students: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Aim/objective This study aimed to classify subgroups of artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety among nursing undergraduates using latent profile analysis, describe their demographic characteristics, and identify factors associated membership in each latent profile. Background Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely implemented in clinical nursing practice, but nursing undergraduates often experience AI anxiety, which impedes their adaptation to smart medical services. Few existing studies have stratified students according to anxiety levels to formulate targeted intervention measures. Design A cross-sectional study. Methods Participants were 526 nursing undergraduates recruited from several medical colleges in Jiangxi, Hunan, Hubei, and Sichuan provinces as well as Chongqing Municipality, China. Questionnaires, including a general information questionnaire, the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Questionnaire, were distributed. Mplus version 8.3 was used for latent profile analysis, and multinomial logistic regression was performed to analyze factors associated with profile membership. Results A total of 526 students were included. The total AI anxiety score was 57.76 ± 15.94, indicating a moderate level of AI anxiety. AI anxiety among undergraduate nursing students was classified into three latent profiles: the low AI anxiety group (53.2%), moderate AI anxiety group (12.7%), and high AI anxiety group (34.0%). Multinomial logistic regression analysis showed that gender, participation in AI-related education or courses, attitude toward AI, and monthly household income (Renminbi [RMB]) were independently associated with membership in latent profiles among undergraduate nursing students with AI anxiety ( p < 0.05). Conclusion Nursing undergraduates present distinct heterogeneous patterns of AI anxiety. These findings may help identify students with elevated AI anxiety and inform individualized educational interventions.

items.title: Learner Agency and the Negotiation of EFL Motivation in GenAI ‐Mediated Drama‐Based Learning: A Qualitative Case Study
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping language learning environments, yet little is known about how it becomes embedded within learners' motivational and agentive experiences in collaborative, informal settings like English drama‐based learning. This qualitative case study examines EFL learners' motivation during a 12‐week GenAI‐mediated English drama production cycle in a Chinese university drama club. Guided by Dörnyei's (2009) L2 Motivational Self System (L2MSS), the analysis examines learners' accounts of the Ideal L2 Self, Ought‐to L2 Self, and L2 Learning Experience alongside three analytic patterns of agency identified in this case: authorship, judgment, and collaboration. Data were drawn from focus groups, individual interviews, drama scripts, GenAI interaction artifacts, and rehearsal observations. Findings indicate that participants experienced GenAI as part of their motivational ecology, particularly in relation to access to advanced language, emerging reference points for “good English,” and the ways collaborative decisions were negotiated. Participants also described different ways of maintaining ownership, evaluating GenAI‐generated language, and coordinating decisions with others. The study extends L2 motivational research by revealing how L2MSS dimensions acquire context‐specific meanings in GenAI‐mediated drama‐based language learning and underscores the importance of fostering critical judgment and sustained human collaboration in GenAI‐supported language learning.

items.title: Learning Analytics and Big Data
items.abstract: Student Engagement refers to the degree to which learners actively participate in educational activities, interact with learning resources, communicate with teachers and peers, and remain involved in the learning process. In digital education, Learning Analytics can provide systematic methods for observing and analysing different forms of student engagement. Traditional measures of engagement often depend on classroom observation, attendance, participation, assignments, and teacher feedback. Digital learning environments can provide additional information through learning management systems, online assessments, discussion platforms, virtual laboratories, educational applications, and connected learning devices. Learning Analytics can transform these data into meaningful information that helps teachers understand patterns of participation and identify opportunities to support student learning. A simplified framework is: Student Activity → Data Collection → Learning Analytics → Engagement Pattern → Teacher Interpretation → Educational SupportThe purpose of engagement analytics should not be simply to count student activities. The central goal is to understand whether students are meaningfully participating in learning and whether additional support may be required. Student engagement represents the learner's active involvement in the educational process. It can include: Participation Attention Interaction Motivation Collaboration Persistence Completion of learning activities Engagement is multidimensional and cannot be completely represented by a single numerical indicator. Student engagement is commonly considered through several dimensions: Behavioural engagement Cognitive engagement Emotional engagement Social engagement These dimensions can interact with one another. Behavioural engagement refers to observable participation in learning activities. Examples include: Attending classes Completing assignments Participating in activities Submitting assessments Accessing learning resources Digital systems can record some of these activities. Cognitive engagement refers to the mental effort students invest in understanding and applying knowledge.

items.title: Learning from Novice Programmers’ Metaphors of Generative Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping how students approach problem-solving in programming education. This study demonstrated the methodological value of metaphor analysis in examining students’ perceptions of AI-supported learning. It explored how first-year students in an introductory Python programming module at a South African university conceptualize GenAI use during coding-related tasks. The context matters because many students from disadvantaged communities enter university with limited computing exposure. Guided by a framework of AI-mediated cognitive engagement, the study drew on 161 responses and used inductive-deductive metaphor analysis to examine how students position AI in relation to their thinking. Six dominant metaphorical framings emerged: tool, tutor, facilitator, specialist, liar, and threat. These metaphors revealed that students experienced AI in both constructive and cautionary ways, as a source of cognitive support and conceptual expansion, and as a potential source of reduced mental effort. The findings showed a systematic correspondence between metaphorical framings and reported cognitive experiences, including mind-mending, mind-stretching, mind-gaming, and mind-replacement. Chi-square and Fisher’s exact tests strengthened the qualitative findings by confirming an association between metaphor roles and cognitive influence. The study contributes to research on AI in education by showing that metaphor offers a powerful lens for understanding how students interpret and regulate AI-supported learning. It argues that GenAI is a conditional cognitive mediator whose impact depends on student agency, epistemic trust, and the nature of engagement. The findings have implications for the design of programming curricula and educational practices, integrating AI responsibly while sustaining critical thinking and academic integrity.

items.title: Make Code as Policy Great Again: Frontier Agents Write, Call, and Evolve Robot Tools
items.abstract: Frontier models can control robots, but reasoning through every reach, grasp, and retreat makes manipulation slow and token-intensive. We revisit code as policy with a different division of labor: models build executable tools, code handles multi-phase motions, and models decide what to do next. We introduce URAI (Universal Robot-Agent Interface), which couples a programming agent that constructs robot tools with an execution agent that uses them in a feedback loop. The programming agent writes reusable and task-specific tools from task intent and refines them through execution feedback and human guidance. The execution agent selects and parameterizes these tools from current observations; each call runs a complete motion locally before returning control to the agent. Unlike delegating subsequent decisions to a generated program, this design retains model-level decision-making between tool executions. Validated tool revisions persist across episodes without updating foundation-model weights, and a shared GUI and API make the same tools available to humans and agents. Across five RoboDojo tasks and four frozen execution agents, URAI raises aggregate success from 18.0% to 53.0% relative to direct fingertip control, with the largest gain on Swap Blocks; with the same tools, a program written in advance reaches only 24% against 56% for two agents deciding after each call. Three of the four agents also finish episodes 1.3-1.5 times faster with 1.5-1.7 times fewer execution-agent output tokens; DeepSeek-V4-Flash's cost barely changes. We further evaluate URAI on seven real-world AgileX dual-arm tasks, spanning object manipulation, cloth folding, and human-interactive tic-tac-toe. URAI connects the coding and decision-making capabilities of frontier agents, organizing robot control around reusable tools that agents can both invoke and revise.
